knowledge_weighting.method: entry-weighted mean of O*NET 31.0 importance (Scale IM): entry targets weight 2; other linked occupations in Job Zone 4 or 5 (or the entry targets' Job Zone) weight 1; Manager, Chief, Postsecondary-faculty, All Other, Supervisor, Director and Treasurers and Controllers titles, and non-target occupations in other Job Zones, weight 0
knowledge_weighting.note: top_knowledge/top_skills are the unweighted mean over all linked occupations (kept for comparison); the outline uses the entry-weighted lists.

skipped_knowledge.reason: service and client-relations knowledge; the outline leaves it to internships, part-time work and the practice tasks rather than a course slot
management and planning knowledge matters most after several years of experience, so the outline gives it no course slot (a management elective is optional)

outline_elements.rule: English Language is placed in Year 1 general education; workplace and management elements (Customer and Personal Service, Administrative, Clerical, Administration and Management, Personnel and Human Resources, Education and Training) get no course slot unless the major's CIP series is about them; the next three elements go to Year 2 and up to three more (ordered by importance to the entry targets) to Year 3; if fewer than two remain for Year 3, knowledge rated at least 2.5 for the entry targets fills it

method.supervisory_tasks: task statement matches a supervisory/managerial pattern (supervise, provide supervision, direct and coordinate, direct the work/activities/staff of, manage staff/personnel/employees/workers/teams, oversee the work/staff, hire, subordinates, assign work to, evaluate the work/performance of, train and supervise); 'under supervision' does not count

quality_flags.note: Authored tier: entry targets and practice tasks were chosen and reviewed per major, so the generated-tier plausibility flags are not applied. Informational only: cited tasks whose O*NET statement is supervisory are listed; their authored scenarios say when they are practice for a later or graduate role.

entry_target_basis: Job Zone 4 linked occupations (excluding Manager/Chief/Postsecondary/All Other/Supervisor/Director/Treasurers and Controllers titles), ranked by similarity of their O*NET knowledge-importance profile to the average profile of the eligible linked occupations (Pearson correlation), base O*NET-SOC .00 codes first; then a documented DreamCo manual override (authored/target_overrides.json) changed the rule output (25-2031.00, 11-9121.02, 11-9121.01) to 25-2031.00, 11-9121.02

entry_target_review.reason: Clinical Research Coordinators was dropped: coordinating clinical trials draws mainly on biology, regulation and patient contact, not physics. The crosswalk links few bachelor's-level physics roles (Physicists is Job Zone 5), so two targets remain: secondary teaching (with a state license) and Water Resource Specialists, whose modeling work uses physics directly.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. You teach high school physics with frequent hands-on labs (carts on ramps, projectile launchers, springs, a low-power laser). Write the classroom rules and routines plan: expectations stated positively, routines for lab groups, equipment checkout and return, a clear stop signal, what happens when a rule is broken during a launch activity, and how you will teach and practice these routines during the first two weeks.

rubric.description: Rules address launch zones, eye protection, laser safety and equipment handling.
Group roles, checkout and return procedures and signals are concrete.
Responses are graduated for general behavior and immediate for safety risks, and routines are rehearsed.

reference_answer_outline: Expectations: respect launch zones, goggles for projectiles and springs, never look into or point the laser at anyone.
Group roles: materials manager, recorder, safety checker.
Checkout sheet; equipment returned and counted before dismissal.
Stop signal: lights off or a bell; hands off equipment.
Safety violation leads to removal from the launch station with an alternative data-analysis task.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. You are the water resource specialist supervising a three-person field crew running a 72-hour pumping test on a new municipal well and taking river-flow measurements nearby to see if pumping affects the river. Write the supervision plan: crew roles and shift schedule, equipment and calibration checks (pressure transducers, flow meter), the measurement schedule, safety (traffic, river wading, electrical generator), data recording and handoffs between shifts, and how you decide to stop or extend the test.

rubric.description: Roles, shifts and handoffs cover 72 hours without gaps or fatigue risks.
Instruments are calibrated and the schedule captures rapid early drawdown and recovery.
Covers field hazards with controls and defines stop or extend criteria.

reference_answer_outline: Three 8-hour shifts with overlap for handoff; supervisor on call.
Transducers in pumping and observation wells, calibrated beforehand; manual checks with a water-level meter.
Log-spaced readings early, then hourly; recovery monitoring after shutdown.
Safety: traffic cones, PFDs and no wading at high flow, generator grounding.
Stop if discharge cannot be held constant or drawdown nears the pump intake.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Before a unit on electric circuits, your physics students will use DC power supplies, breadboards, multimeters and small resistors that can get hot. Plan the instruction and supervision: a short demonstration of correct use, the common mistakes that cause injury or damage (short circuits, wrong meter setting), a 'license' check each student passes before independent use, how you position yourself and monitor during lab time, and what to do if a component overheats.

rubric.description: Explains correct use of power supplies and meters (current limit, measuring current in series, voltage in parallel).
Students show competence in a check before independent use.
Describes monitoring strategies and a clear response to overheating or smoke.

reference_answer_outline: Demo: set current limit low, build circuit with power off, check before switching on.
Mistakes: meter on current setting across a source, shorted leads, touching hot resistors.
License check: build a simple circuit and measure voltage and current correctly.
Teacher circulates with a scan pattern; groups raise a card for a circuit check.
Overheating: switch off at the supply, do not touch, let cool, report.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Plan a 50-minute physics lesson on Newton's second law. Include a demonstration (for example, a cart pulled by a hanging mass with a motion sensor or phone accelerometer), a short explanation that connects net force, mass and acceleration, a discussion that confronts the common belief that motion requires a continuing force, and a quick formative check. Explain how students use the demonstration's data in the explanation.

rubric.description: Correctly relates net force, mass and acceleration and addresses the force-implies-motion misconception.
The demonstration produces data (acceleration for different masses) that students analyze.
Includes a meaningful check, such as predicting acceleration for a new mass, and adapts based on results.

reference_answer_outline: Prediction prompt before the demo.
Demo: vary hanging mass and cart mass; record acceleration.
Plot acceleration against net force for constant mass; slope relates to mass.
Discussion: a hockey puck on ice keeps moving without a push.
Check: two quick prediction problems with mini whiteboards.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Invented case: in a drought year, your regional water authority needs an extra 2 million cubic meters over the summer, and a neighboring irrigation district holds senior rights to the river. Prepare a negotiation brief: each side's interests and constraints, your best alternative if no deal is reached, options for a deal (temporary lease, fallowing payments, exchange of treated wastewater, dry-year option contracts), how you would value the water, legal or regulatory approvals required, and how you will communicate with affected farmers and residents.

rubric.description: Identifies interests of both sides, not just positions, and a realistic alternative to agreement.
Proposes several deal structures with a reasoned price range.
Notes required approvals under water law and plans fair, transparent communication.

reference_answer_outline: Authority interests: reliable summer supply, cost; district interests: crop income, long-term rights, community.
Alternative: emergency conservation and groundwater pumping.
Options: one-year lease, payments for fallowing specific fields, recycled water exchange, multi-year dry-year option.
Value using farm net income lost plus a premium; compare with alternative supply cost.
Approvals from the state water agency; public meetings and written FAQs.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A town wants to know whether a grassy drainage channel can carry the peak runoff from a new 12-hectare housing development. Using stated, labeled assumptions, estimate the peak flow with the rational method (runoff coefficient, rainfall intensity for the design storm, area), then use Manning's equation to check whether a trapezoidal channel with given dimensions and slope can carry it. Show all calculations, discuss the sensitivity of the answer to the runoff coefficient and roughness, and state when a more detailed model would be needed.

rubric.description: Rational method and Manning's equation are applied with consistent units and correct geometry.
Shows how the result changes with plausible ranges of runoff coefficient and roughness.
Explains when a hydrograph or computer model (such as for larger areas or storage) is required.

reference_answer_outline: Peak flow equals C times i times A with unit conversion; e.g. C around 0.5 for suburban lots.
Channel area and hydraulic radius for the trapezoid; Manning flow with n around 0.03 to 0.04 for grass.
Compare capacity with peak flow; freeboard.
Sensitivity table for C and n.
Rational method is limited to small catchments; use hydrograph modeling for detention design.
